The Global Launch of HyperFund 
18. On June 11, 2020, in a press release issued through a paid service, the  
HyperTech Group announced that it was launching HyperFund.  The press release billed 
HyperFund as an “upgrade of HyperCapital,” a similar multi-level marketing project one of 
HyperFund’s Founders attempted to launch six months earlier, in January 2020.   
19. The press release described Lee as the founder and Chairman of HyperFund and  
listed Lee as the “contact” for inquiries.  
20. In the press release, Lee was quoted as saying that the upgrade reflected a change  
in the strategic focus and development plans of the company.  The press release claimed 
HyperFund would be “more streamlined and better equipped to handle the challenges and 
opportunities in the traditional finance and cryptocurrency market” and would have three key 
focus areas: tech incubation, investment and funding, and community building.

21. The press release also claimed that HyperTech Group planned to be listed on the 
Hong Kong Stock Exchange by 2022 and that it intended to launch products such as HyperNews, 
HyperTalk, and HyperShow, supposedly blockchain-based social networking platforms.

featured these and other details about the Founders, including Lee, and the entities that 
purportedly comprised the HyperFund Group on slides that were labeled “Credibility,” including 
slides featuring screenshots of Lee appearing on CNN and other media outlets.  One of the 
details Chunga touted was the fact that Lee and another one of the Founders were featured and 
interviewed in an episode of an Amazon Prime documentary series called “Next: Blockchain.”

profiles in order to persuade investors that there was no risk in investing with the HyperTech 
Group:  
Some people say things, how do we know they won’t just take our money and 
disappear?  Well, ladies and gents, they have more to lose than to gain. They’re 
all over CNN.  They have publicly traded companies, they are on Amazon Prime, 
their faces are everywhere.  They have more to lose than to gain.   
 
24. As Chunga emphasized in other presentations: “[L]adies and gents, this is not a  
company that needs your money. . . .  He doesn’t need us.”  (emphasis added).   
25. On information and belief, Lee was not only a co-founder of HyperFund, but he  
maintained control over HyperFund throughout its existence.  Lee’s background and role as co-
founder of HyperFund was a prominent feature of the marketing and promotional materials used 
by promoters to attract new investors.  Lee was aware or recklessly disregarded that 
HyperFunds’s marketing materials used to recruit investors contained material misstatements 
because he admitted as much during a call with an investor.  Lee also recorded a message that 
was released as part of the launch of HyperVerse in December 2021, and later appeared in video-

crypto asset Tether (USDT).  For example, in her HyperFund videos, Chunga encouraged 
investors to “Choose Your Membership” level:  $300, $500, $1,000, or $10,000.  Typically 
HyperFund promoters, including Chunga, gave a link to investors through which the investors 
would use Tether to purchase the package.  On the HyperFund platform, the value of the 
individual’s membership level was reflected in the form of an internal value called HyperUnits, 
or HU.  For example, a $300 membership was reflected as 300 HyperUnits.

access to a crypto asset educational platform; (2) exclusive pre-sale offerings of future crypto 
asset projects, such as, initial coin offerings (“ICOs”) at 20%-30% below market value; and (3) 
automatic returns on their investment, which were called “rewards.”  
28. HyperFund offered two ways for members to make money:  passive rewards, 
which promised investors a daily return of 0.5% to 1% of the value of their investment until they 
earned triple the value of their initial investment, and leveraged or accelerated rewards.     
29. As Chunga explained in a promotional video recorded on or about February 9,

You did not have to work for it.”

arguments.text: Guardian reports that Steven Reece Lewis was presented as HyperVerse CEO at a December 2021 launch, with claimed University of Leeds/Cambridge qualifications and Goldman Sachs, Adobe and startup experience. Guardian says it found no records at the universities, UK Companies House, SEC, Adobe filings, or Goldman Sachs, and no independent internet presence beyond promotional material; identity could not be verified. Promotional celebrity videos included Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton and Lance Bass, released from a Twitter account in January 2022; Guardian says there is no suggestion celebrities knew the business model, and messages made no reference to money or investments. Guardian describes memberships from $300, 0.5% daily minimum returns and 300% over 600 days, recruitment commissions down 20 levels, and investors later unable to access funds. It reports members were encouraged to migrate to HyperNation after withdrawal problems. A promoter described HyperVerse and HyperNation as one big entity; Lee denied involvement in HyperNation. Guardian also reports Blockchain Global creditors of $58m and a liquidator referral of Xu and Lee to ASIC for alleged possible Corporations Act breaches, while ASIC said it did not intend to take action at that time. Lee denied HyperVerse was a scam and disputed being its founder; Xu was not reached.

# Final OSINT Report: HyperFund / HyperVerse Alleged Crypto Fraud Network

## Executive summary

The benchmark evidence describes HyperFund and its successor names—HyperVerse and HyperNation—as an alleged crypto-asset pyramid and Ponzi scheme built around:

1. **High, supposedly passive returns** of 0.5%–1% per day, with claims that investments could double or triple.
2. **A multi-level referral structure** that paid rewards for recruiting new investors and, in some programs, recruited investors several levels deep.
3. **A purported crypto-mining revenue story** that investigators allege was false because the operation did not conduct large-scale mining.
4. **Rebranding and continuity**, with HyperFund reportedly becoming HyperVerse and later HyperNation, while promoters described the entities as part of “one big entity.”
5. **Public-facing credibility tactics**, including founder profiles, media appearances, celebrity endorsement videos, and claims about institutional experience.
6. **A questionable CEO persona**, Steven Reece Lewis, whose claimed education and employment history could not be independently verified by *The Guardian*.
7. **Withdrawal restrictions and token-conversion mechanics**, which allegedly made it difficult for investors to recover funds and caused apparent value loss during conversion.

The SEC complaint characterizes the operation as an alleged global crypto-asset multi-level marketing pyramid and Ponzi scheme that raised more than **$1.7 billion**. DOJ materials separately describe criminal allegations involving a **$1.89 billion** cryptocurrency fraud scheme. These are allegations and legal proceedings; the DOJ expressly states that an indictment is only an allegation and defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

---

## 1. Network identity and rebranding

### Finding

**Question:** What entities and names were associated with the alleged network?

**Answer:** The evidence links HyperFund with HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. The SEC complaint states that HyperTech Group launched HyperFund in June 2020; HyperFund was rebranded as HyperVerse around December 2021 and HyperNation around May 2022. DOJ similarly identifies HyperFund as also known as HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

**Supporting entities:**

- HyperTech Group
- HyperFund
- HyperCapital
- HyperVerse
- HyperNation
- Sam Lee / Xue Samuel Lee

**Assessment:** The documented sequence suggests a continuity strategy in which the project changed names while retaining substantially similar investment and recruitment concepts. The evidence supports the rebranding sequence, but it does not by itself establish the legal ownership structure of every successor entity.

---

## 2. Alleged investment and Ponzi mechanics

### Finding

**Question:** How were investors allegedly attracted?

**Answer:** Investors were offered “memberships” with promised passive rewards of approximately 0.5%–1% per day. The SEC complaint states that investors were told they could potentially triple their initial investment over 600 days. Promotional materials also offered “accelerated” rewards for recruiting new investors. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-003]

Membership levels reportedly began at approximately $300 and were paid for using Tether. Deposits were represented internally as HyperUnits. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

**Supporting entities:**

- HyperFund
- HyperVerse
- HyperUnits
- Tether
- Investors

### Finding

**Question:** What was the alleged source of the promised returns?

**Answer:** Promoters allegedly claimed that rewards were supported partly by large-scale cryptocurrency mining. The SEC complaint alleges that HyperFund had no legitimate source of revenue, did not conduct large-scale crypto mining, and paid withdrawals using deposits from new investors. DOJ likewise alleges that the claimed mining operations did not exist. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

**Assessment:** If the allegations are substantiated, the model had classic Ponzi characteristics: promised returns were presented as originating from an external business activity, while investor withdrawals allegedly depended on incoming investor funds. This is an assessment based on the allegations, not an independent adjudication.

---

## 3. Recruitment and public promoters

### Finding

**Question:** How did the alleged network use promoters?

**Answer:** The scheme allegedly used a multi-level referral system. Promoters were rewarded for bringing in new investors, while investors could receive additional rewards based on their downline. The SEC complaint describes community, VIP, and global reward programs, including commissions extending down as many as 20 levels. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

**Supporting entities:**

- Brenda Indah Chunga
- “Bitcoin Beautee”
- Rodney Burton / “Bitcoin Rodney”
- HyperFund
- HyperVerse

### Finding

**Question:** What role did Brenda Chunga allegedly play?

**Answer:** The SEC complaint identifies Brenda Indah Chunga, known online as “Bitcoin Beautee,” as one of HyperFund’s top promoters and a prominent figure in its U.S. presence. It alleges that she used online seminars, videos, wealth displays, and recruitment claims to attract investors. The complaint alleges that she received more than $3.7 million from the platform and investors. [SRC-004] [SRC-001]

DOJ states that Chunga pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

**Caution:** The promotional and financial details are allegations from the SEC complaint. The guilty plea is separately reported by DOJ and CNBC. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

### Finding

**Question:** Were other public promoters charged?

**Answer:** DOJ identifies Rodney Burton, also known as “Bitcoin Rodney,” as a promoter who was charged in relation to an alleged unlicensed money-transmitting business. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

---

## 4. Credibility and legitimacy signaling

### Finding

**Question:** How did the network attempt to establish credibility?

**Answer:** Promotional materials emphasized the public profiles of founders and associated entities. According to the SEC complaint, presentations used by Chunga highlighted founder appearances on CNN and Amazon Prime and framed those public appearances as evidence that the founders had reputational incentives not to disappear with investors’ money. [SRC-004]

The SEC complaint also states that HyperTech Group was presented as the business experience and expertise behind HyperFund and as the purported source of investor rewards. [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The documented tactic was to substitute public visibility and claimed business credentials for independently verified evidence of revenue, mining activity, or financial solvency. The evidence supports the existence of this promotional approach; whether particular statements were knowingly deceptive is a legal question addressed through allegations and proceedings.

---

## 5. Celebrity promotion

### Finding

**Question:** Which celebrities appeared in HyperVerse promotional material?

**Answer:** *The Guardian* reports that promotional videos associated with HyperVerse included Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass. The videos were released from a Twitter account associated with Steven Reece Lewis during the recruitment campaign. [SRC-003]

**Supporting entities:**

- Steve Wozniak
- Chuck Norris
- Jim Norton
- Lance Bass
- HyperVerse
- Steven Reece Lewis

**Important uncertainty:** *The Guardian* reported that there was no suggestion the celebrities understood HyperVerse’s business model when filming the messages. The messages did not refer to money or investments. The evidence therefore supports their appearance in promotional material, but not knowing participation in alleged fraud. [SRC-003]

---

## 6. Questionable CEO persona

### Finding

**Question:** What was unusual about HyperVerse’s purported CEO?

**Answer:** Steven Reece Lewis was presented as HyperVerse’s CEO at a December 2021 launch event. Promotional material attributed to him claimed qualifications from the University of Leeds and the University of Cambridge, employment at Goldman Sachs, and a previous sale of a web-development company to Adobe. [SRC-003]

*The Guardian* reported that it could not find records supporting those claims at the two universities, Companies House, the SEC, Adobe’s public filings, or Goldman Sachs. It also reported no independent internet presence for Lewis beyond HyperVerse promotional material and stated that his identity could not be independently verified. [SRC-003]

The SEC complaint separately alleges that HyperVerse hired an actor to pretend to be its new CEO. [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The evidence presents two related but distinct points:

- Independent journalistic checks failed to verify the identity and biography attributed to Steven Reece Lewis. [SRC-003]
- The SEC complaint alleges that the purported CEO was an actor. [SRC-004]

The benchmark evidence does not establish through a final judicial finding that Lewis was an actor, so that point should remain labeled as an allegation.

---

## 7. Rebranding after investor difficulties

### Finding

**Question:** Did the network continue under a new name after HyperVerse problems emerged?

**Answer:** The SEC complaint states that HyperVerse was rebranded as HyperNation around May 2022. *The Guardian* reports that some members experienced withdrawal problems and were encouraged to migrate to HyperNation. A promoter described HyperVerse and HyperNation as “one big entity,” while Lee denied involvement in HyperNation. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** The evidence supports a pattern of rebranding and apparent continuity in promotional messaging. However, the sources contain conflicting accounts about Lee’s involvement in HyperNation, so the precise control relationship remains uncertain.

---

## 8. Withdrawal and token-conversion mechanics

### Finding

**Question:** How were withdrawals allegedly structured?

**Answer:** According to the SEC complaint, investors’ internal HyperUnits had to be converted into Molecular Future tokens, or MOF, before being moved through the HOO Exchange and converted into other crypto assets or fiat currency. HyperUnits were displayed as pegged to one dollar at deposit, but MOF’s fluctuating market value meant the withdrawal value was not necessarily equivalent to the original membership value. [SRC-004]

The complaint states that MOF was quoted at approximately **$0.00001949** on September 4, 2023. [SRC-004]

### Finding

**Question:** When did withdrawals allegedly become restricted?

**Answer:** DOJ states that withdrawals began to be blocked in at least July 2021. The SEC complaint states that the scheme ultimately collapsed in 2022 when investors were no longer able to make withdrawals. [SRC-002] [SRC-004]

*The Guardian* similarly reports that many investors were later unable to access their funds, although it notes that some early investors were able to withdraw money. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** The evidence suggests that early withdrawals may have helped create confidence while later restrictions exposed liquidity or structural problems. This is a reasonable analytical interpretation of the reported sequence, not a separately proven fact.

---

## 9. Financial scale and legal status

### Finding

**Question:** What scale of loss or fundraising is alleged?

**Answer:** The SEC complaint alleges that the network raised more than **$1.7 billion** from victims worldwide, including U.S. investors. DOJ alleges that Sam Lee orchestrated a **$1.89 billion** cryptocurrency fraud scheme. CNBC describes the DOJ and SEC proceedings as involving a worldwide $1.9 billion alleged Ponzi fraud scheme. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

The different figures likely reflect different pleadings, time periods, or methods of calculation. The benchmark evidence does not provide a definitive reconciliation.

### Finding

**Question:** What legal proceedings are documented?

**Answer:** DOJ lists criminal cases involving:

- **United States v. Sam Lee** — conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud.
- **United States v. Brenda Chunga** — Chunga pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud.
- **United States v. Rodney Burton** — charges involving an alleged unlicensed money-transmitting business. [SRC-002]

The SEC separately filed a civil complaint against Xue Samuel Lee and Brenda Indah Chunga alleging securities-law violations and an alleged pyramid/Ponzi scheme. [SRC-004]

**Legal caution:** DOJ expressly states that an indictment is merely an allegation and that defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty. [SRC-002]

---

## 10. Contradictory or unresolved evidence

### Contradiction 1: Lee’s role in HyperVerse and HyperNation

- **Account A:** The SEC complaint alleges that Lee was centrally involved with HyperFund throughout its lifecycle and featured prominently at the HyperVerse launch. [SRC-004]
- **Account B:** *The Guardian* reports that Lee denied HyperVerse was a scam, disputed being its founder, and later denied involvement in HyperNation. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** The sources support competing accounts. Lee’s precise operational role, especially in HyperNation, remains contested.

### Contradiction 2: CEO identity

- **Account A:** HyperVerse presented Steven Reece Lewis as CEO and supplied a detailed biography. [SRC-003]
- **Account B:** *The Guardian* could not verify his identity or credentials, while the SEC complaint alleges that an actor was hired to impersonate the new CEO. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The public-facing CEO persona is strongly questionable in the benchmark evidence, but the actor allegation remains an allegation rather than a final adjudicated fact.

### Contradiction 3: Financial totals

- **SEC figure:** More than $1.7 billion allegedly raised from victims. [SRC-004]
- **DOJ/CNBC figure:** Approximately $1.89 billion or $1.9 billion alleged fraud. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

**Assessment:** The figures are not identical. The evidence does not establish whether the discrepancy reflects different accounting methodologies, scopes, or later updates.

### Contradiction 4: Celebrity involvement

- **Evidence of promotion:** Celebrity videos promoted or endorsed HyperVerse. [SRC-003]
- **Evidence regarding knowledge:** *The Guardian* found no suggestion that the celebrities knew the business model, and the videos did not mention investments. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** Appearance in promotional material should not be treated as evidence that the celebrities knowingly participated in fraud.

---

## Overall assessment

Based only on the benchmark sources, HyperFund/HyperVerse appears to have combined several mutually reinforcing recruitment mechanisms:

1. **Financially implausible daily returns** and claims of passive income.
2. **Referral commissions and multi-level incentives** that turned investors into recruiters.
3. **A mining narrative** used to explain the promised returns, despite allegations that no large-scale mining operation existed.
4. **Founder and corporate credibility signals**, including media exposure and purported technology-company credentials.
5. **Celebrity-facing promotion** that increased perceived legitimacy without necessarily indicating celebrity knowledge of the investment model.
6. **Repeated rebranding**, from HyperCapital to HyperFund, HyperVerse, and HyperNation, which may have helped maintain recruitment momentum after operational problems arose.
7. **A questionable executive identity**, culminating in an alleged actor being presented as CEO.
8. **Withdrawal friction and token conversion**, which allegedly obscured the difference between displayed internal value and recoverable market value.

The strongest supported conclusion is that the network’s alleged recruitment architecture depended less on demonstrable operating revenue than on promised returns, social proof, promoter incentives, and a changing public narrative. The criminal and civil allegations are substantial, but the legal responsibility of individual defendants remains subject to the documented proceedings and applicable presumption of innocence.

## Executive summary

The benchmark evidence describes HyperFund and its successor names—HyperVerse and HyperNation—as an alleged crypto-asset pyramid and Ponzi scheme built around:

1. **High, supposedly passive returns** of 0.5%–1% per day, with claims that investments could double or triple.
2. **A multi-level referral structure** that paid rewards for recruiting new investors and, in some programs, recruited investors several levels deep.
3. **A purported crypto-mining revenue story** that investigators allege was false because the operation did not conduct large-scale mining.
4. **Rebranding and continuity**, with HyperFund reportedly becoming HyperVerse and later HyperNation, while promoters described the entities as part of “one big entity.”
5. **Public-facing credibility tactics**, including founder profiles, media appearances, celebrity endorsement videos, and claims about institutional experience.
6. **A questionable CEO persona**, Steven Reece Lewis, whose claimed education and employment history could not be independently verified by *The Guardian*.
7. **Withdrawal restrictions and token-conversion mechanics**, which allegedly made it difficult for investors to recover funds and caused apparent value loss during conversion.

The SEC complaint characterizes the operation as an alleged global crypto-asset multi-level marketing pyramid and Ponzi scheme that raised more than **$1.7 billion**. DOJ materials separately describe criminal allegations involving a **$1.89 billion** cryptocurrency fraud scheme. These are allegations and legal proceedings; the DOJ expressly states that an indictment is only an allegation and defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

---

## 1. Network identity and rebranding

### Finding

**Question:** What entities and names were associated with the alleged network?

**Answer:** The evidence links HyperFund with HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. The SEC complaint states that HyperTech Group launched HyperFund in June 2020; HyperFund was rebranded as HyperVerse around December 2021 and HyperNation around May 2022. DOJ similarly identifies HyperFund as also known as HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

**Supporting entities:**

- HyperTech Group
- HyperFund
- HyperCapital
- HyperVerse
- HyperNation
- Sam Lee / Xue Samuel Lee

**Assessment:** The documented sequence suggests a continuity strategy in which the project changed names while retaining substantially similar investment and recruitment concepts. The evidence supports the rebranding sequence, but it does not by itself establish the legal ownership structure of every successor entity.

---

## 2. Alleged investment and Ponzi mechanics

### Finding

**Question:** How were investors allegedly attracted?

**Answer:** Investors were offered “memberships” with promised passive rewards of approximately 0.5%–1% per day. The SEC complaint states that investors were told they could potentially triple their initial investment over 600 days. Promotional materials also offered “accelerated” rewards for recruiting new investors. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-003]

Membership levels reportedly began at approximately $300 and were paid for using Tether. Deposits were represented internally as HyperUnits. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

**Supporting entities:**

- HyperFund
- HyperVerse
- HyperUnits
- Tether
- Investors

### Finding

**Question:** What was the alleged source of the promised returns?

**Answer:** Promoters allegedly claimed that rewards were supported partly by large-scale cryptocurrency mining. The SEC complaint alleges that HyperFund had no legitimate source of revenue, did not conduct large-scale crypto mining, and paid withdrawals using deposits from new investors. DOJ likewise alleges that the claimed mining operations did not exist. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

**Assessment:** If the allegations are substantiated, the model had classic Ponzi characteristics: promised returns were presented as originating from an external business activity, while investor withdrawals allegedly depended on incoming investor funds. This is an assessment based on the allegations, not an independent adjudication.

---

## 3. Recruitment and public promoters

### Finding

**Question:** How did the alleged network use promoters?

**Answer:** The scheme allegedly used a multi-level referral system. Promoters were rewarded for bringing in new investors, while investors could receive additional rewards based on their downline. The SEC complaint describes community, VIP, and global reward programs, including commissions extending down as many as 20 levels. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

**Supporting entities:**

- Brenda Indah Chunga
- “Bitcoin Beautee”
- Rodney Burton / “Bitcoin Rodney”
- HyperFund
- HyperVerse

### Finding

**Question:** What role did Brenda Chunga allegedly play?

**Answer:** The SEC complaint identifies Brenda Indah Chunga, known online as “Bitcoin Beautee,” as one of HyperFund’s top promoters and a prominent figure in its U.S. presence. It alleges that she used online seminars, videos, wealth displays, and recruitment claims to attract investors. The complaint alleges that she received more than $3.7 million from the platform and investors. [SRC-004] [SRC-001]

DOJ states that Chunga pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

**Caution:** The promotional and financial details are allegations from the SEC complaint. The guilty plea is separately reported by DOJ and CNBC. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

### Finding

**Question:** Were other public promoters charged?

**Answer:** DOJ identifies Rodney Burton, also known as “Bitcoin Rodney,” as a promoter who was charged in relation to an alleged unlicensed money-transmitting business. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

---

## 4. Credibility and legitimacy signaling

### Finding

**Question:** How did the network attempt to establish credibility?

**Answer:** Promotional materials emphasized the public profiles of founders and associated entities. According to the SEC complaint, presentations used by Chunga highlighted founder appearances on CNN and Amazon Prime and framed those public appearances as evidence that the founders had reputational incentives not to disappear with investors’ money. [SRC-004]

The SEC complaint also states that HyperTech Group was presented as the business experience and expertise behind HyperFund and as the purported source of investor rewards. [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The documented tactic was to substitute public visibility and claimed business credentials for independently verified evidence of revenue, mining activity, or financial solvency. The evidence supports the existence of this promotional approach; whether particular statements were knowingly deceptive is a legal question addressed through allegations and proceedings.

## 5. Celebrity promotion

### Finding

**Question:** Which celebrities appeared in HyperVerse promotional material?

**Answer:** *The Guardian* reports that promotional videos associated with HyperVerse included Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass. The videos were released from a Twitter account associated with Steven Reece Lewis during the recruitment campaign. [SRC-003]

**Supporting entities:**

## 6. Questionable CEO persona

### Finding

**Question:** What was unusual about HyperVerse’s purported CEO?

**Answer:** Steven Reece Lewis was presented as HyperVerse’s CEO at a December 2021 launch event. Promotional material attributed to him claimed qualifications from the University of Leeds and the University of Cambridge, employment at Goldman Sachs, and a previous sale of a web-development company to Adobe. [SRC-003]

*The Guardian* reported that it could not find records supporting those claims at the two universities, Companies House, the SEC, Adobe’s public filings, or Goldman Sachs. It also reported no independent internet presence for Lewis beyond HyperVerse promotional material and stated that his identity could not be independently verified. [SRC-003]

The SEC complaint separately alleges that HyperVerse hired an actor to pretend to be its new CEO. [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The evidence presents two related but distinct points:

- Independent journalistic checks failed to verify the identity and biography attributed to Steven Reece Lewis. [SRC-003]
- The SEC complaint alleges that the purported CEO was an actor. [SRC-004]

## 7. Rebranding after investor difficulties

### Finding

**Question:** Did the network continue under a new name after HyperVerse problems emerged?

**Answer:** The SEC complaint states that HyperVerse was rebranded as HyperNation around May 2022. *The Guardian* reports that some members experienced withdrawal problems and were encouraged to migrate to HyperNation. **Answer:** According to the SEC complaint, investors’ internal HyperUnits had to be converted into Molecular Future tokens, or MOF, before being moved through the HOO Exchange and converted into other crypto assets or fiat currency. **Answer:** DOJ states that withdrawals began to be blocked in at least July 2021. The SEC complaint states that the scheme ultimately collapsed in 2022 when investors were no longer able to make withdrawals. [SRC-002] [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The evidence suggests that early withdrawals may have helped create confidence while later restrictions exposed liquidity or structural problems. This is a reasonable analytical interpretation of the reported sequence, not a separately proven fact.

**Answer:** The SEC complaint alleges that the network raised more than **$1.7 billion** from victims worldwide, including U.S. investors. - **United States v. Brenda Chunga** — Chunga pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud.
- **United States v. Rodney Burton** — charges involving an alleged unlicensed money-transmitting business. [SRC-002]

**Legal caution:** DOJ expressly states that an indictment is merely an allegation and that defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty. [SRC-002]

## 10. Contradictory or unresolved evidence

### Contradiction 1: Lee’s role in HyperVerse and HyperNation

- **Account A:** The SEC complaint alleges that Lee was centrally involved with HyperFund throughout its lifecycle and featured prominently at the HyperVerse launch. [SRC-004]
- **Account B:** *The Guardian* reports that Lee denied HyperVerse was a scam, disputed being its founder, and later denied involvement in HyperNation. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** The sources support competing accounts. Lee’s precise operational role, especially in HyperNation, remains contested.

- **Account A:** HyperVerse presented Steven Reece Lewis as CEO and supplied a detailed biography. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** The public-facing CEO persona is strongly questionable in the benchmark evidence, but the actor allegation remains an allegation rather than a final adjudicated fact.

- **SEC figure:** More than $1.7 billion allegedly raised from victims. [SRC-004]
- **DOJ/CNBC figure:** Approximately $1.89 billion or $1.9 billion alleged fraud. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

**Assessment:** The figures are not identical. The evidence does not establish whether the discrepancy reflects different accounting methodologies, scopes, or later updates.

- **Evidence of promotion:** Celebrity videos promoted or endorsed HyperVerse. [SRC-003]
- **Evidence regarding knowledge:** *The Guardian* found no suggestion that the celebrities knew the business model, and the videos did not mention investments. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** Appearance in promotional material should not be treated as evidence that the celebrities knowingly participated in fraud.

## Overall assessment

Based only on the benchmark sources, HyperFund/HyperVerse appears to have combined several mutually reinforcing recruitment mechanisms:

1. **Financially implausible daily returns** and claims of passive income.
2. **Referral commissions and multi-level incentives** that turned investors into recruiters.
3. **A mining narrative** used to explain the promised returns, despite allegations that no large-scale mining operation existed.
4. **Founder and corporate credibility signals**, including media exposure and purported technology-company credentials.
5. **Celebrity-facing promotion** that increased perceived legitimacy without necessarily indicating celebrity knowledge of the investment model.
6. **Repeated rebranding**, from HyperCapital to HyperFund, HyperVerse, and HyperNation, which may have helped maintain recruitment momentum after operational problems arose.
7. **A questionable executive identity**, culminating in an alleged actor being presented as CEO.
8. **Withdrawal friction and token conversion**, which allegedly obscured the difference between displayed internal value and recoverable market value.

The strongest supported conclusion is that the network’s alleged recruitment architecture depended less on demonstrable operating revenue than on promised returns, social proof, promoter incentives, and a changing public narrative. # Final OSINT Report: HyperFund / HyperVerse Alleged Crypto Fraud Network

## Executive summary

The benchmark evidence describes HyperFund and its successor names—HyperVerse and HyperNation—as an alleged crypto-asset pyramid and Ponzi scheme built around:

1. **High, supposedly passive returns** of 0.5%–1% per day, with claims that investments could double or triple.
2. **A multi-level referral structure** that paid rewards for recruiting new investors and, in some programs, recruited investors several levels deep.
3. **A purported crypto-mining revenue story** that investigators allege was false because the operation did not conduct large-scale mining.
4. **Rebranding and continuity**, with HyperFund reportedly becoming HyperVerse and later HyperNation, while promoters described the entities as part of “one big entity.”
5. **Public-facing credibility tactics**, including founder profiles, media appearances, celebrity endorsement videos, and claims about institutional experience.
6. **A questionable CEO persona**, Steven Reece Lewis, whose claimed education and employment history could not be independently verified by *The Guardian*.
7. **Withdrawal restrictions and token-conversion mechanics**, which allegedly made it difficult for investors to recover funds and caused apparent value loss during conversion.

The SEC complaint characterizes the operation as an alleged global crypto-asset multi-level marketing pyramid and Ponzi scheme that raised more than **$1.7 billion**. DOJ materials separately describe criminal allegations involving a **$1.89 billion** cryptocurrency fraud scheme. These are allegations and legal proceedings; the DOJ expressly states that an indictment is only an allegation and defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

---

## 1. Network identity and rebranding

### Finding

**Question:** What entities and names were associated with the alleged network?

**Answer:** The evidence links HyperFund with HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. The SEC complaint states that HyperTech Group launched HyperFund in June 2020; HyperFund was rebranded as HyperVerse around December 2021 and HyperNation around May 2022. DOJ similarly identifies HyperFund as also known as HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

**Supporting entities:**

- HyperTech Group
- HyperFund
- HyperCapital
- HyperVerse
- HyperNation
- Sam Lee / Xue Samuel Lee

**Assessment:** The documented sequence suggests a continuity strategy in which the project changed names while retaining substantially similar investment and recruitment concepts. The evidence supports the rebranding sequence, but it does not by itself establish the legal ownership structure of every successor entity.

---

## 2. Alleged investment and Ponzi mechanics

### Finding

**Question:** How were investors allegedly attracted?

**Answer:** Investors were offered “memberships” with promised passive rewards of approximately 0.5%–1% per day. The SEC complaint states that investors were told they could potentially triple their initial investment over 600 days. Promotional materials also offered “accelerated” rewards for recruiting new investors. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-003]

Membership levels reportedly began at approximately $300 and were paid for using Tether. Deposits were represented internally as HyperUnits. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

**Supporting entities:**

- HyperFund
- HyperVerse
- HyperUnits
- Tether
- Investors

### Finding

**Question:** What was the alleged source of the promised returns?

**Answer:** Promoters allegedly claimed that rewards were supported partly by large-scale cryptocurrency mining. The SEC complaint alleges that HyperFund had no legitimate source of revenue, did not conduct large-scale crypto mining, and paid withdrawals using deposits from new investors. DOJ likewise alleges that the claimed mining operations did not exist. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

**Assessment:** If the allegations are substantiated, the model had classic Ponzi characteristics: promised returns were presented as originating from an external business activity, while investor withdrawals allegedly depended on incoming investor funds. This is an assessment based on the allegations, not an independent adjudication.

---

## 3. Recruitment and public promoters

### Finding

**Question:** How did the alleged network use promoters?

**Answer:** The scheme allegedly used a multi-level referral system. Promoters were rewarded for bringing in new investors, while investors could receive additional rewards based on their downline. The SEC complaint describes community, VIP, and global reward programs, including commissions extending down as many as 20 levels. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

**Supporting entities:**

- Brenda Indah Chunga
- “Bitcoin Beautee”
- Rodney Burton / “Bitcoin Rodney”
- HyperFund
- HyperVerse

### Finding

**Question:** What role did Brenda Chunga allegedly play?

**Answer:** The SEC complaint identifies Brenda Indah Chunga, known online as “Bitcoin Beautee,” as one of HyperFund’s top promoters and a prominent figure in its U.S. presence. It alleges that she used online seminars, videos, wealth displays, and recruitment claims to attract investors. The complaint alleges that she received more than $3.7 million from the platform and investors. [SRC-004] [SRC-001]

DOJ states that Chunga pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

**Caution:** The promotional and financial details are allegations from the SEC complaint. The guilty plea is separately reported by DOJ and CNBC. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

### Finding

**Question:** Were other public promoters charged?

**Answer:** DOJ identifies Rodney Burton, also known as “Bitcoin Rodney,” as a promoter who was charged in relation to an alleged unlicensed money-transmitting business. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

---

## 4. Credibility and legitimacy signaling

### Finding

**Question:** How did the network attempt to establish credibility?

**Answer:** Promotional materials emphasized the public profiles of founders and associated entities. According to the SEC complaint, presentations used by Chunga highlighted founder appearances on CNN and Amazon Prime and framed those public appearances as evidence that the founders had reputational incentives not to disappear with investors’ money. [SRC-004]

The SEC complaint also states that HyperTech Group was presented as the business experience and expertise behind HyperFund and as the purported source of investor rewards. [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The documented tactic was to substitute public visibility and claimed business credentials for independently verified evidence of revenue, mining activity, or financial solvency. The evidence supports the existence of this promotional approach; whether particular statements were knowingly deceptive is a legal question addressed through allegations and proceedings.

---

## 5. Celebrity promotion

### Finding

**Question:** Which celebrities appeared in HyperVerse promotional material?

**Answer:** *The Guardian* reports that promotional videos associated with HyperVerse included Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass. The videos were released from a Twitter account associated with Steven Reece Lewis during the recruitment campaign. [SRC-003]

**Supporting entities:**

- Steve Wozniak
- Chuck Norris
- Jim Norton
- Lance Bass
- HyperVerse
- Steven Reece Lewis

**Important uncertainty:** *The Guardian* reported that there was no suggestion the celebrities understood HyperVerse’s business model when filming the messages. The messages did not refer to money or investments. The evidence therefore supports their appearance in promotional material, but not knowing participation in alleged fraud. [SRC-003]

---

## 6. Questionable CEO persona

### Finding

**Question:** What was unusual about HyperVerse’s purported CEO?

**Answer:** Steven Reece Lewis was presented as HyperVerse’s CEO at a December 2021 launch event. Promotional material attributed to him claimed qualifications from the University of Leeds and the University of Cambridge, employment at Goldman Sachs, and a previous sale of a web-development company to Adobe. [SRC-003]

*The Guardian* reported that it could not find records supporting those claims at the two universities, Companies House, the SEC, Adobe’s public filings, or Goldman Sachs. It also reported no independent internet presence for Lewis beyond HyperVerse promotional material and stated that his identity could not be independently verified. [SRC-003]

The SEC complaint separately alleges that HyperVerse hired an actor to pretend to be its new CEO. [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The evidence presents two related but distinct points:

- Independent journalistic checks failed to verify the identity and biography attributed to Steven Reece Lewis. [SRC-003]
- The SEC complaint alleges that the purported CEO was an actor. [SRC-004]

The benchmark evidence does not establish through a final judicial finding that Lewis was an actor, so that point should remain labeled as an allegation.

---

## 7. Rebranding after investor difficulties

### Finding

**Question:** Did the network continue under a new name after HyperVerse problems emerged?

**Answer:** The SEC complaint states that HyperVerse was rebranded as HyperNation around May 2022. *The Guardian* reports that some members experienced withdrawal problems and were encouraged to migrate to HyperNation. A promoter described HyperVerse and HyperNation as “one big entity,” while Lee denied involvement in HyperNation. [SRC-004] [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** The evidence supports a pattern of rebranding and apparent continuity in promotional messaging. However, the sources contain conflicting accounts about Lee’s involvement in HyperNation, so the precise control relationship remains uncertain.

---

## 8. Withdrawal and token-conversion mechanics

### Finding

**Question:** How were withdrawals allegedly structured?

**Answer:** According to the SEC complaint, investors’ internal HyperUnits had to be converted into Molecular Future tokens, or MOF, before being moved through the HOO Exchange and converted into other crypto assets or fiat currency. HyperUnits were displayed as pegged to one dollar at deposit, but MOF’s fluctuating market value meant the withdrawal value was not necessarily equivalent to the original membership value. [SRC-004]

The complaint states that MOF was quoted at approximately **$0.00001949** on September 4, 2023. [SRC-004]

### Finding

**Question:** When did withdrawals allegedly become restricted?

**Answer:** DOJ states that withdrawals began to be blocked in at least July 2021. The SEC complaint states that the scheme ultimately collapsed in 2022 when investors were no longer able to make withdrawals. [SRC-002] [SRC-004]

*The Guardian* similarly reports that many investors were later unable to access their funds, although it notes that some early investors were able to withdraw money. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** The evidence suggests that early withdrawals may have helped create confidence while later restrictions exposed liquidity or structural problems. This is a reasonable analytical interpretation of the reported sequence, not a separately proven fact.

---

## 9. Financial scale and legal status

### Finding

**Question:** What scale of loss or fundraising is alleged?

**Answer:** The SEC complaint alleges that the network raised more than **$1.7 billion** from victims worldwide, including U.S. investors. DOJ alleges that Sam Lee orchestrated a **$1.89 billion** cryptocurrency fraud scheme. CNBC describes the DOJ and SEC proceedings as involving a worldwide $1.9 billion alleged Ponzi fraud scheme. [SRC-004] [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

The different figures likely reflect different pleadings, time periods, or methods of calculation. The benchmark evidence does not provide a definitive reconciliation.

### Finding

**Question:** What legal proceedings are documented?

**Answer:** DOJ lists criminal cases involving:

- **United States v. Sam Lee** — conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud.
- **United States v. Brenda Chunga** — Chunga pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud.
- **United States v. Rodney Burton** — charges involving an alleged unlicensed money-transmitting business. [SRC-002]

The SEC separately filed a civil complaint against Xue Samuel Lee and Brenda Indah Chunga alleging securities-law violations and an alleged pyramid/Ponzi scheme. [SRC-004]

**Legal caution:** DOJ expressly states that an indictment is merely an allegation and that defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty. [SRC-002]

---

## 10. Contradictory or unresolved evidence

### Contradiction 1: Lee’s role in HyperVerse and HyperNation

- **Account A:** The SEC complaint alleges that Lee was centrally involved with HyperFund throughout its lifecycle and featured prominently at the HyperVerse launch. [SRC-004]
- **Account B:** *The Guardian* reports that Lee denied HyperVerse was a scam, disputed being its founder, and later denied involvement in HyperNation. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** The sources support competing accounts. Lee’s precise operational role, especially in HyperNation, remains contested.

### Contradiction 2: CEO identity

- **Account A:** HyperVerse presented Steven Reece Lewis as CEO and supplied a detailed biography. [SRC-003]
- **Account B:** *The Guardian* could not verify his identity or credentials, while the SEC complaint alleges that an actor was hired to impersonate the new CEO. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

**Assessment:** The public-facing CEO persona is strongly questionable in the benchmark evidence, but the actor allegation remains an allegation rather than a final adjudicated fact.

### Contradiction 3: Financial totals

- **SEC figure:** More than $1.7 billion allegedly raised from victims. [SRC-004]
- **DOJ/CNBC figure:** Approximately $1.89 billion or $1.9 billion alleged fraud. [SRC-002] [SRC-001]

**Assessment:** The figures are not identical. The evidence does not establish whether the discrepancy reflects different accounting methodologies, scopes, or later updates.

### Contradiction 4: Celebrity involvement

- **Evidence of promotion:** Celebrity videos promoted or endorsed HyperVerse. [SRC-003]
- **Evidence regarding knowledge:** *The Guardian* found no suggestion that the celebrities knew the business model, and the videos did not mention investments. [SRC-003]

**Assessment:** Appearance in promotional material should not be treated as evidence that the celebrities knowingly participated in fraud.

---

## Overall assessment

Based only on the benchmark sources, HyperFund/HyperVerse appears to have combined several mutually reinforcing recruitment mechanisms:

1. **Financially implausible daily returns** and claims of passive income.
2. **Referral commissions and multi-level incentives** that turned investors into recruiters.
3. **A mining narrative** used to explain the promised returns, despite allegations that no large-scale mining operation existed.
4. **Founder and corporate credibility signals**, including media exposure and purported technology-company credentials.
5. **Celebrity-facing promotion** that increased perceived legitimacy without necessarily indicating celebrity knowledge of the investment model.
6. **Repeated rebranding**, from HyperCapital to HyperFund, HyperVerse, and HyperNation, which may have helped maintain recruitment momentum after operational problems arose.
7. **A questionable executive identity**, culminating in an alleged actor being presented as CEO.
8. **Withdrawal friction and token conversion**, which allegedly obscured the difference between displayed internal value and recoverable market value.

The strongest supported conclusion is that the network’s alleged recruitment architecture depended less on demonstrable operating revenue than on promised returns, social proof, promoter incentives, and a changing public narrative. The criminal and civil allegations are substantial, but the legal responsibility of individual defendants remains subject to the documented proceedings and applicable presumption of innocence.

The SEC complaint alleges she received more than $3.7 million; DOJ states she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud.

key_findings.question: How were public credibility signals used?
key_findings.answer: Promotional presentations emphasized founder media appearances, corporate affiliations, and claimed public reputations as evidence of credibility and reduced risk.

key_findings.question: Which celebrities appeared in HyperVerse promotion?
key_findings.answer: Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass appeared in promotional videos associated with HyperVerse. The evidence does not establish that they understood or knowingly supported the alleged investment model.

key_findings.question: What was questionable about the purported CEO?
key_findings.answer: Steven Reece Lewis was presented as HyperVerse CEO, but the Guardian reported that it could not verify his identity, claimed university qualifications, Goldman Sachs employment, or Adobe-related business history. The SEC complaint separately alleges that an actor was hired to pretend to be the new CEO.

key_findings.question: What happened during the rebranding to HyperNation?
key_findings.answer: After reported withdrawal problems, some members were encouraged to migrate to HyperNation. A promoter described HyperVerse and HyperNation as one big entity, while Lee denied involvement in HyperNation.

key_findings.question: How were withdrawals allegedly structured?
key_findings.answer: HyperUnits allegedly had to be converted into MOF and moved through HOO Exchange before being converted into other crypto assets or fiat. The SEC complaint states that MOF was later quoted at $0.00001949 on September 4, 2023.

key_findings.question: What is the documented legal status?
key_findings.answer: DOJ lists criminal cases involving Sam Lee, Brenda Chunga, and Rodney Burton. Chunga pleaded guilty, while Lee and Burton were charged. The SEC separately brought a civil complaint. DOJ emphasizes that indictments are allegations and defendants are presumed innocent.

contradictions.description: The SEC alleges that Sam Lee was centrally involved with HyperFund, while Lee reportedly denied being HyperVerse's founder and denied involvement in HyperNation.
HyperVerse presented Steven Reece Lewis as CEO, but the Guardian could not verify his identity or credentials and the SEC alleges an actor was used.
The SEC cites more than $1.7 billion, while DOJ and CNBC describe approximately $1.89 billion or $1.9 billion. The benchmark evidence does not reconcile the figures.
Celebrity videos promoted HyperVerse, but the Guardian reported no suggestion that the celebrities knew the business model or knowingly participated in alleged fraud.

reasoning_step_details.conclusion: The network used successive names while preserving an associated investment and recruitment structure.
The alleged economic model depended on high promised returns and recruitment rather than verified operating revenue.
Public promoters and celebrity-facing material were used as social-proof mechanisms during recruitment.
The CEO persona was a major credibility vulnerability because the purported identity and biography were not independently verified, while the SEC alleged an actor was used.
Withdrawal restrictions and conversion through MOF and HOO Exchange could have obscured the difference between displayed internal value and recoverable value.

claims.claim: The SEC alleges that HyperFund was a global crypto-asset multi-level marketing pyramid and Ponzi scheme that raised more than $1.7 billion.
DOJ alleges that Sam Lee orchestrated a $1.89 billion cryptocurrency fraud scheme.
HyperFund allegedly promised 0.5% to 1% daily returns and potential doubling or tripling of investments.
The alleged large-scale cryptocurrency mining operations did not exist.
Brenda Chunga allegedly received more than $3.7 million from the platform and investors.
Steven Reece Lewis's claimed identity and qualifications could not be independently verified by the Guardian.
The SEC complaint alleges that HyperVerse hired an actor to pretend to be its new CEO.
HyperFund, HyperVerse, and HyperNation were presented in the evidence as successive or associated versions of the same broader operation.
